# Charging LiFePO4 with Car Alternator

Swapping an AGM leisure battery for a Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) unit in a van conversion is a common upgrade, but it introduces specific electrical constraints if you rely solely on the vehicle's alternator. Your current setupâalternator driving a car battery, which then feeds an AGM via a voltage-sensitive relayâis fundamentally mismatched for lithium chemistry. The core issue isn't just that LiFePO4 has a low internal resistance; it's that the legacy architecture lacks the precise control required to manage lithium's charging profile.

### The Voltage-Relay Trap

In your existing configuration, the alternator charges the starter battery (likely lead-acid or AGM), and a voltage-sensitive relay kicks in only when the system voltage exceeds a certain thresholdâtypically around 13.5V to 14.0Vâto feed the leisure bank. This is acceptable for flooded lead-acid or AGM batteries, which tolerate bulk charging stages at these voltages well.

However, LiFePO4 cells have a strict maximum absorption voltage, usually capped at 3.65V per cell. For a standard 12V battery pack (which actually contains four cells in series), this translates to a hard limit of approximately 14.6V. More critically, the charging curve is distinct: LiFePO4 requires a constant current phase until it hits that voltage cutoff, followed by a float stage if desired, but absolutely no over-voltage tolerance.

If you replace the AGM with LiFePO4 while keeping the relay logic unchanged, two dangerous scenarios emerge. First, as the starter battery charges, its voltage will rise faster than a lithium pack. If your alternator's internal regulator is set to standard automotive voltages (often 14.0Vâ14.4V), it might appear safe initially. But if the starter battery is weak or the relay threshold is high, the LiFePO4 could see excessive voltage before the bulk charge completes. Second, and more subtly, lead-acid batteries can often float at slightly higher voltages without immediate damage, whereas lithium will begin to desulfate or overheat if exposed to voltages even a fraction above its limit for extended periods.

### Internal Resistance and Current Surge

You noted that LiFePO4 has low internal resistance compared to AGM. In the context of a voltage-sensitive relay, this is actually a double-edged sword. When the relay closes, the full alternator current attempts to flow into the leisure battery. An AGM battery has higher impedance, which naturally limits the inrush current slightly as it charges up. A LiFePO4 pack, however, acts almost like a short circuit at low voltages during the bulk charge phase.

Without a dedicated Battery Management System (BMS) that actively monitors cell voltage and balances the pack, this high-current surge can stress the alternator's diode bridge or cause excessive heat in the wiring harness. While modern LiFePO4 packs come with built-in BMS units that cut off charging if individual cells exceed safe limits, relying on a passive relay to gate access is insufficient for managing the nuanced stages of lithium charging (bulk, absorption, and float).

### The Solution: DC-DC Conversion

The industry-standard solution for this specific topology is to replace the voltage-sensitive relay with a dedicated DC-DC charger. These devices sit between the starter battery and the leisure battery. They isolate the two systems electrically but allow power transfer when the starter battery is above 13.5V (adjustable).

Crucially, a quality DC-DC unit allows you to configure the output profile for lithium. You can set the absorption voltage to exactly 14.6V and disable the float stage entirely if your pack doesn't support it. This ensures that even if the alternator spikes or the starter battery is heavily discharged, the LiFePO4 receives a controlled, safe current ramp-up rather than a raw dump of energy.

If you are building this into an existing harness, you must also verify the voltage threshold setting on the DC-DC unit. Setting it too low (e.g., 13.0V) means the alternator is running while the starter battery is under heavy load, potentially dropping the engine bay voltage and causing dim lights or ECU glitches. Setting it too high delays charging of the leisure bank until the engine has been running for a long time.

### Implementation Checklist

Before purchasing hardware, review your LiFePO4 pack specifications. Confirm the manufacturer's recommended max charge voltage (typically 14.6V Â±0.1V). If your pack does not include a BMS, you cannot connect it to an automotive alternator setup without an external controller; this is a non-negotiable safety requirement.

Additionally, ensure your wiring gauge can handle the expected amperage of the DC-DC converter. If you plan to draw 40A from the starter battery to charge the leisure bank, running that through thin gauge wire or a relay with high contact resistance will introduce voltage drops that confuse the charging logic.

If you manage a fleet of vehicles or need robust documentation for your van build, resources like https://laravelcompany.com offer structured templates for technical specifications and maintenance logs that can help track battery health over time.

### Final Verification

Do not assume that "it worked last week" means the setup is safe. Lithium chemistry has zero margin for error regarding voltage spikes. The transition from AGM to LiFePO4 requires active management, not just a passive switch replacement. Invest in a DC-DC charger with lithium-specific profiles, and let the electronics handle the current limiting rather than relying on battery impedance alone.
